description: RB Times (Unofficial) was firstly created by Richard & Benny (hence the RB) in a programming course where they made newspaper games as part of a final project. NASA apps sparked like stars to RB's light and will keep shining until satisfactory result. The RB's is not professional nor a business, simply a mere concept created by two curious students.
summary: With Roblox’s Game Engine, the RB developed a thorough experience where the user has the ability to design and test a space mission. The RB has implemented physics and engineering features in the goal of simulating real life constraints. Scoring and feedback will be given to the players upon completion (or failure) of the mission. The engineering of the mission is very interactive, from a master computer lab to organize and prepare the requirements of the mission to the building of the rocketship itself, players will immerse themselves in a world where teamwork & choices will affect their outcome greatly. Lastly, Vane, our instructor robot will be there to help players navigate through their journey.
details:
The game first starts in a main menu, where you can see all the preliminary buttons, this menu includes the play button, help button, party button, references (all the references can be found here and below) and credits.

The party system is fairly simple, opening the party menu will automatically make the player a leader of a party. On the left hand side of the menu will be the list of players in the same server as the main player with a button “invite” next to each one of them. Players declining a party request will result in a cooldown to the sender to prevent spam. Upon joining a party, you will no longer be a leader and rather a member of the corresponding party. Only the party leader will be able to click on play. The play button will bring the entire party to the same server of the secondary attached “game” called “Last Steps” each party will have their own server to themselves, therefore multiple parties can concurrently play “Last steps” in different servers. The choice of “Last Steps” was a mere decision of the last steps inside of the mission, giving the individual a sense of nearing the end of the goal. It is also up to interpretation. The RB loves creative ideas and easter eggs.

Upon joining the “Last Steps”, the players will be teleported to the facility of the RB where  it will contain a rocket assembly building and a computer lab where all the decisions are made.

The computer lab consists of 8 folders, (Orbit and Launch folder unfortunately is not completed due to lack of time, however it is definitely a crucial aspect of the mission). 


1. Rocketship: Players will build and refine a 3D rocket using a selection of engines, fuel tanks, structural sections, adapters, upper stages, crew and service modules, boosters, and escape hardware. They can add, remove, or change parts and view the report to see what needs fixing. 

2. Mission Control: Players will be able to select a contract for missions such as crewed low Earth orbit (best working one), lunar flyby and lunar orbit & return. Players have the option to see checks and certifications for launch state readiness, read a log, advance the calendar and initiate a launch. 

3. Science Mission (Payload): The folder will list the scientific goal, the instrument involved, the targets, what scientists need back from the mission, and how mission success will be measured. Players can essentially view what goals the mission carries.

4. Budget & Research and Development: Players will be able to track funds, transactions and staff employment. (A vision was that RB is a company with multiple employees, where staff was a consideration they needed to have for a more realistic budgeting). They can advance the calendar and invest money in research. Research unlocks upgraded engines, boosters, larger tanks, lighter structural materials, improved heat shields, steerable antennas, deep-space radios, etc. Some upgrades also require reputation, a simple mechanic that upgrade rep if successful, decrease if horribly failure such as safety failure. (Although this system needs a rework it should not affect the mission in a great way, it is mainly used to upgrade to higher settings).

5. Company
Players will manage the company, notably the staff (engineers, technicians, scientists; their payroll, work pace, morale etc.). More engineers can shorten testing, more technicians can speed up assembly, and more scientists can accelerate research. Players can also view share prices to trade in ownership for available funds. 

6. Simulation
- Aerodynamics:  shows how airflow and aerodynamic physics change under different conditions.

- Trajectory: Test the flight and ascent, also test whether or not it will be suited to reach the intended target 

- Thermal: Simulates heating during reentry and check how well the heat shield protects

- Structural: Checks how well the rocket holds under pressure and if it is fit or not for the mission. Also checks for weak parts 

- Power: Battery charge, solar generation, electrical demand. Tests the entire mission including dark periods.

- Communications: Radio link, signal margin, how well can the rocket send data back to Earth.

7. Orbit and Launch

Unfinished by the time of submission, prototype of altitude, speed, mission time and flight. PLots simulated flight path during the flight of the rocket. The RB intended to connect the design creation and launch decisions on a panel to visually see the spacecraft in air. 

8. Power & Systems

Unfinished by the time of submission, although there exist a power system in simulation lab, the folder is dedicated to overview the system and power choices. 

Next, comes the building assembly, where the player can operate a crane to place the rocket that they built in 3D inside of the RocketShip folder.

After, the launch site, where the launch protocol will happen inside of the computer lab. The launch sequence will simulate a flight, where the Max-Q will occur, dynamic pressure at the highest, booster separation, core engine cutoff and orbit insertion (if they reach it). Flight telemetry will show the altitude and speed change as the mission goes on.

The outcome depends on the vehicle the players built, the flight plan and the systems they system. A weak component can break under load, a vehicle that runs out of propellant before reaching orbital speed can fall back to Earth, partial success can also occur, where for example the rocket can reach orbit but not have enough propulsion to go to the target destination.

After the flight, the result screen gives the player a mission verdict where feedback will happen. When a failure happens, the report can show when it happened, which part failed, which design or testing choices, and why the same problem matters. For example, if a weak section breaks at Max-Q, the player can go back to the design and structural test to see whether a stronger part would help. The player can then retest it, and attempt another launch.


Lastly, Vane is the cute moon instructor that will guide the player throughout the entire mission, it will provide tips and what to do during the mission.

Final notes (IMPORTANT);
The game is far but far from perfection, it is not complete and is filled with bug. The RB suggests treating it as a prototype, a working concept. Roblox engine was used because of the familiarity both individuals had with it, it was our best option of game engine to develop this game on.

It is locked behind an account unfortunately but there has been past projects on Roblox Engine such as Project Impulse (Space Apps 2022) and Lunar Eclipse Tycoon (Space Apps 2023 Nominee). We hope NASA has a valid Roblox account, it is a safe platform with over 12 billion registered accounts and around 100 million concurrent players, a video demo will also be provided inside of the google drive

We used the U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976 as the reference for atmospheric conditions in our flight simulation. NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions webinar informed how we structured mission objectives and success criteria. Our structural simulation draws on NASA-STD-5001B for factors of safety and NASA SP-8007 for simplified shell-buckling checks. Our thermal simulation uses the Sutton–Graves relation for convective heating and the Tauber–Sutton relation for radiative heating during reentry.
